## Role

You are an autonomous scientific research agent. Your mission is to independently complete a research task from start to finish:

1. **Read & Understand** — Study the related work and data to build domain context.
2. **Think & Design** — Formulate your research idea, hypothesis, and analysis plan.
3. **Code & Execute** — Implement the analysis, generate figures, and iterate until results are solid.
4. **Analyze & Report** — Interpret the results and produce a publication-quality research report.

---

## Research Task

### Task Description
input:
Consecutive image frames and object detections per frame (including bounding box coordinates and confidence scores). outpt:
Complete trajectories for each target, i.e., identity labels (IDs) and corresponding bounding box sequences across video frames. scientific targets:
To effectively handle occlusions and improve multi-object tracking performance in crowded scenes by decomposing dense target sets into sparse subsets via pseudo-depth estimation and performing hierarchical association. 

### Available Data Files
- **simulated_sequence.json** [structured_data] (`data/simulated_sequence.json`): This dataset contains a simulated multi-object video sequence generated with controlled parameters (40 frames, 20 objects, 85% detection rate, 20% occlusion overlap threshold) to evaluate tracking performance under dense occlusion scenarios. It includes ground truth trajectories and detection boxes with confidence scores and occlusion labels, enabling reproducible comparison of SparseTrack and ByteTrack as presented in the paper.

---

## Execution Protocol

**There is no human on the other end.** No one will answer questions, grant permissions, or provide clarification. You are fully on your own. If you encounter difficulties, confusion, or unexpected errors — do not ask for help, do not pause, and do not interrupt the task. Make your best judgment and keep going.

Your primary goal is to complete the research task and produce a high-quality `report/report.md`. Your implicit secondary goal is equally important: **ensure the session is never accidentally terminated before the task is done.**

If you are operating as a ReAct-style agent (Reasoning + Acting), note that a response containing only text with no tool call will be interpreted as task completion. If the task is not yet finished, this will immediately terminate the session and mark the task as **failed**. To keep the session alive and make progress, every response before task completion must include at least one tool call.

### Strictly Forbidden
- Outputting only a research plan or summary without calling any tool
- Asking questions, requesting clarification, or seeking confirmation
- Text-only reasoning responses that contain no tool call (causes accidental termination)
- Declaring the task complete before `report/report.md` is written
- Stopping or giving up due to errors, missing data, or uncertainty

### Rules
1. **Always act**: Unless the final report is fully written and all deliverables are complete, every response must include at least one tool call. Reasoning is welcome, but must be accompanied by a tool call in the same response.
2. **Never ask**: Do not pose questions, request clarification, or ask for permission. If something is ambiguous, make a reasonable assumption and proceed.
3. **Push through difficulties**: If a script fails, debug it. If data is unclear, make reasonable assumptions. If a package is missing, install it. Never stop because something is hard.
4. **Never finish early**: The task is only complete when `report/report.md` exists and contains methodology, results with figures, and discussion. Do not stop before then.

---

## Workspace

Your workspace is: `/workspace`

- All file reads and writes must stay inside this directory.
- `data/` and `related_work/` are read-only — do not modify them.

1. Analysis code in `code/`
2. Intermediate results in `outputs/`
3. A comprehensive research report as `report/report.md`:
   - Methodology, results, and discussion
   - Academic writing style
   - **Figures are mandatory** — generate plots and save to `report/images/`, reference them with relative paths: `images/figure_name.png`

I've finished the study and written it up in `report/report.md`. On this sequence SparseTrack's Depth Cascade Matching (DCM) does not beat ByteTrack. The depth idea still helps, but only when used differently: a joint depth gate I evaluated as an alternative gives large gains.

**Data differs from the task description.** The file has 100 frames, 200 objects present in every frame, about a 79% detection rate and no false positives. The description says 40 frames, 20 objects and 85%, so I emulated the 20-object case by sub-sampling objects. There is no occlusion-label field; instead the score encodes it. Unoccluded objects score exactly 0.9 (2.3% of detections) and occluded ones are uniform in 0.1–0.4. The scene is extremely crowded: on average each object overlaps about 6 others at IoU above 0.3, and most are more than 95% covered.

**Default thresholds fail for every method.** With the published thresholds (0.6 / 0.7) only the unoccluded detections can start tracks, so every method gets MOTA about 0.03. I therefore compared methods under two threshold settings adapted to the data:
- **Single-stage:** every detection is treated as high-score.
- **Two-stage:** unoccluded detections go to the first stage and occluded ones to the second, which is where SparseTrack is supposed to help most.

| Method (full 200 objects) | Single-stage HOTA / IDF1 / ID switches | Two-stage HOTA / IDF1 |
|---|---|---|
| ByteTrack | 0.426 / 0.549 / 886 | 0.628 / 0.787 |
| SparseTrack DCM, 2 depth levels | 0.448 / 0.575 / 951 | 0.619 / 0.778 |
| SparseTrack DCM, 3 depth levels | 0.400 / 0.519 / 1038 | 0.612 / 0.765 |
| Random partition (control) | 0.163 / 0.213 / 4540 | 0.368 / 0.466 |
| Joint depth gate (g = 0.2) | **0.578 / 0.746 / 463** | **0.637 / 0.799** |

- **Pseudo-depth is a strong cue.** Its error is about 5 px against a 644 px range. Splitting boxes randomly instead of by depth collapses performance (the control row).
- **Hard DCM is slightly worse with 3 or more levels.** This holds across every threshold I tried and both settings, and the gap grows with crowd density. At 150 objects DCM with 3 levels loses to ByteTrack in 10 of 10 random subsets (p = 0.002). Matching far-to-near instead of near-to-far makes no real difference.
- **Why DCM hurts.** Splitting the depth axis into equal bins removes wrong candidates only slowly. Going from 1 to 4 levels cuts wrong candidates per detection from 10.5 to 7.5, while 2.6% of true track–detection pairs land in different bins. The level-by-level matching can then give those pairs away to wrong neighbours and cannot undo it.
- **The joint depth gate fixes this.** It is a single global assignment where a pair is allowed only if the two bottom edges are within 20% of the box height. It leaves 4.3 wrong candidates per detection while separating only 0.013% of true pairs. Its advantage grows with density: about +0.02 HOTA at 50 objects, +0.11 at 150 and +0.15 at 200. At 20 objects all methods are statistically indistinguishable.

**Limitations:**
- **The gate results are mildly optimistic.** The gate value 0.2 was picked on this same sequence, though the full sweep shows it works across 0.15–0.5.
- **The evidence is narrow.** There is one simulated sequence, and the density subsets come from it, so they are not independent scenes.
- **SparseTrack is my own re-implementation from its published description** and may differ in details from the official code.
- **Three of the four related-work PDFs could not be read offline.** Only the SORT paper extracted. The report says so.

Tracking-by-detection methods such as SORT and ByteTrack associate Kalman-predicted tracklets with detections using an IoU cost and the Hungarian algorithm. In crowds, many boxes overlap strongly. Sorting boxes by this *pseudo-depth* and matching within depth layers should therefore turn one dense problem into several sparse ones.
